content: Boeing has won its biggest order from a Chinese airline in nearly a decade, after Xiamen Airlines agreed on Tuesday to buy 50 of the American planemaker's 737-8 Max jets in a deal worth about $7.4 billion at list prices. The agreement, announced by Xiamen Airlines' parent company China Southern Airlines in a stock exchange filing, marks the first major purchase of Boeing aircraft by a Chinese carrier in years — and a significant thaw in a market that had gone almost entirely quiet for the US manufacturer. According to Reuters, China Southern said its subsidiary signed the agreement with Boeing on November 24, with the 50 single-aisle jets scheduled for delivery in batches between 2031 and 2034. The deal still needs approval from Xiamen Airlines' shareholders and from the relevant Chinese government authorities before it can take effect, the filing said. The headline figure of $7.4 billion reflects the list price of the aircraft, including airframes and engines. As is standard in the industry, Boeing granted a substantial discount, so the actual amount Xiamen Airlines will pay is considerably lower — a figure the filing did not disclose. China Southern's board approved the proposal by eight votes to none on November 24 and agreed to submit it to shareholders. The order matters far beyond its size. China is the world's second-largest aviation market and, over the next two decades, is expected to need thousands of new aircraft as its airlines expand and replace ageing fleets. Yet Boeing has barely sold a new jet there in years. Chinese carriers largely stopped placing fresh Boeing orders amid the trade tensions between Washington and Beijing, and deliveries of already-ordered aircraft were repeatedly delayed or redirected. European rival Airbus, by contrast, has steadily deepened its footprint in China, including a final assembly line in Tianjin, and has taken the lion's share of recent Chinese orders. That makes the Xiamen deal the clearest sign yet that the freeze is easing. It is the largest order from a Chinese airline since 2017, according to news reports, and it comes just weeks after a tentative framework discussed during the recent diplomatic contacts between Washington and Beijing raised hopes of a much larger Chinese commitment — one that, at the time, was expected to cover as many as 500 jets, both single-aisle and widebody models. That broader deal has not been formalised, and the Xiamen order, while substantial, falls well short of those expectations. Still, industry analysts see it as a meaningful first step rather than a one-off. Xiamen Airlines, based in the southeastern port city of Xiamen, is one of China's largest carriers and a long-standing Boeing customer. Its fleet is built overwhelmingly around the 737, and the 737-8 — the latest generation of Boeing's workhorse single-aisle family — fits its network of domestic and regional routes across China and Southeast Asia. The aircraft, seating around 170 passengers in a typical two-class layout, is designed for the short and medium-haul flying that dominates Xiamen's operations. The timing of the deliveries, spread from 2031 to 2034, also tells a story. Boeing's order book is full for years ahead, and the long lead time reflects both the manufacturer's production backlog and the airline's own fleet planning horizon. For Boeing, the order adds valuable long-term backlog at a moment when it is working to stabilise production of the 737 Max after years of disruption, and it gives the company a foothold to argue for more Chinese orders in the years ahead. The deal also carries a political dimension that neither side will want to overstate. Aircraft orders have long been used as a barometer — and occasionally as a bargaining chip — in US-China trade relations, with large purchases often timed to coincide with diplomatic milestones. The Xiamen agreement arrives as the two countries continue to manage a fragile trade truce, and it will be read in both capitals as evidence that commercial ties, at least in aviation, are resuming. Whether it opens the door to the far larger orders once discussed remains an open question. For now, Boeing has something it has lacked in China for years: a new, signed, major order. And Xiamen Airlines has secured the aircraft it needs to grow through the next decade — at a price, as the filing made clear, well below the sticker. summary: Xiamen Airlines has agreed to buy 50 Boeing 737-8 Max jets worth about $7.4 billion at list prices, the largest order from a Chinese carrier since 2017 and the first major Chinese purchase from Boeing in years, with deliveries scheduled from 2031 to 2034.
title: Boeing wins $7.4 billion order for 50 jets from China's Xiamen Airlines, its biggest Chinese deal since 2017
